Finding: Ticket price tiers for live shows: 50p was a cheap gig, about £2 the average price for a reasonably big band, £3.50 for a Wembley supergig
Includes: Face value only; VAT and box-office commission deducted separately
Proposed gameplay use: Set gig revenue by venue tier and cap ticket escalation; derive venue break-even from capacity x price
Notes / caveats: Article is established-act scale; tiers themselves are scene-wide

Finding: Of each ticket, about one third went to the promoter, plus 8% VAT and box-office commission, before the band's share
Includes: Promoter cut, VAT, box-office commission
Proposed gameplay use: Deduct promoter cut and VAT from gross gig receipts before band payout
Notes / caveats: 8% VAT figure matches the 1974-79 UK standard rate

Finding: 10cc commanded about £1,000 per gig, but about £750 was spent before the band reached the stage (crew wages, hotels, petrol, vehicles, publicity)
Includes: Costs cover road crew, hotels, petrol, vehicle purchase/depreciation, publicity
Proposed gameplay use: Model a per-show cost stack that grows with crew, transport and PA size - a large fee can still be a loss
Notes / caveats: Famous act - not beginner-representative; fee is an established-act ceiling

Finding: Gallagher & Lyle self-financed a 29-person tour for £15,000 and recovered only about £3,000, counting it worthwhile because album sales doubled
Includes: 29 people on the road; hotels £3,500, orchestra wages £5,000, lorry + coach £1,500
Proposed gameplay use: Tours can be financed at a loss as promotion; make 'tour pays off in record sales' a real trade-off
Notes / caveats: Famous act - not beginner-representative

Finding: By 1973 London pub venues (Hope and Anchor, Nashville, Tally Ho) were drawing crowds for pub-rock bands; the circuit stayed the entry rung into the punk era (Stranglers played regular 'residency' gigs mid-1976)
Includes: n/a
Proposed gameplay use: Name the pub tier as the game's first bookable rung and keep it alive through 1976
Notes / caveats: Residency detail: themeninblack.co.uk forum interview (anecdote)

Finding: Festival economics of the era were fragile: Isle of Wight 1970 drew 600,000-700,000 but was declared free after organisers saw no profit; Glastonbury 1970 charged £1 for 1,500 people; Bickershaw 1972 sold £2.25 tickets for a ~£60,000 gate yet lost money, with passout resale and a collapsed financier leaving acts unpaid
Includes: Gate receipts; organiser losses and unpaid acts reported
Proposed gameplay use: Festival events can leak revenue (passout resale) and fail on counterparty risk (unpaid acts); mega-festivals can be declared free
Notes / caveats: Companions: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight_Festival_1970 ; bbc.com/news/newsbeat-33109564 (Glastonbury)

Finding: Earnings baselines for opportunity-cost balancing: full-time men (New Earnings Survey) averaged £26.8/week manual and £35.8/week non-manual in 1970, rising to £55.7 and £68.4 by 1975; the all-employees series runs £17.51/week (1970 Q1) to £74.41/week (1979 Q4)
Includes: Gross weekly earnings (series differ by definition)
Source type: Government statistical digest; official statistics series
Proposed gameplay use: Use the manual-worker series as the day-job opportunity cost a band member quits; label the series in-game
Notes / caveats: All-employees series source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/AWEPPUKQ (recommended baseline for the decade's drift)

Finding: Musicians' Union negotiated 1970s rates (non-live): recording session £24.75 for 3 hours; ILR radio session £15 (Capital Radio paid £30); London theatre salaries £50-£58.50/week; member subscriptions £8-£29/year
Unit / coverage: Per musician; per session or per week
Includes: Union-negotiated minimum rates for studio/broadcast/theatre work
Proposed gameplay use: Anchor professional session and theatre work rates; gives musicians a non-gig income option
Notes / caveats: Page does not date each figure within the decade; no pub/club rate appears

Finding: The dole as income floor: unemployment benefit for a man with a dependent wife and four children was £27.50-£34.30/week (1976) against average manual earnings of £66.97/week; benefit was contribution-based, requiring Class 1 contributions on earnings at least 25x the weekly lower earnings limit (£15 for 1977-78); UB40 named themselves after the signing-on form (1978)
Includes: Benefit only; upper figure includes earnings-related supplement
Proposed gameplay use: Model the dole as a modest pre-success income floor (~40-50% of a wage) gated on a prior work record
Notes / caveats: Eligibility threshold: hansard.parliament.uk/commons/1977-11-18/debates/b41cd3fa-c09b-4fed-afe5-9506998fd72f/UnemploymentBenefit. Single-claimant rate not located

Finding: Classified ad: used Vox AC50 amp offered at £45 and a T60 bass speaker cabinet at £25; a new AC50 Super Twin had retailed at £184 in 1965
Includes: Secondhand amplifier and cabinet
Proposed gameplay use: Secondhand backline around £45-70 in 1970; new gear is a multi-month wage outlay, so used-gear trading matters
Notes / caveats: Only isolated period gear price found; broader instrument price data remains a gap

Finding: Desperate Bicycles made a single for £153 total for 500 copies (3 hours studio time, pressing, sleeves) and made £210 profit on the first pressing; a 1,000 repress sold out in a fortnight
Includes: Studio hire, pressing, sleeves
Proposed gameplay use: Cheapest viable release tier: a self-financed single in the low hundreds of pounds that can recoup in months

Finding: Scritti Politti printed their accounts on the sleeve: recording at Spaceward £98 (14 hrs incl. master tape), mastering £40 (lacquer cut), pressing £369.36 (2,500 copies at 13p + £27 plating), labels £8
Includes: Itemised: studio time; lacquer; pressing; labels (sleeve printing extra, not itemised)
Proposed gameplay use: Unit-cost breakdown for indie pressing; a second side doubles cutting cost unless both tracks share one cut

Finding: Buzzcocks borrowed about £750 from friends and family to pay for the first pressing (1,000 copies) of Spiral Scratch, recorded in one session of 3 hours tracking + 2 hours mixing on 16-track
Includes: Recording and manufacturing (no itemised split)
Proposed gameplay use: Self-release budget baseline between F11 (bare £153) and a small label deal
Notes / caveats: Accounts elsewhere give ~£500 - see unresolved list

Finding: Two-tier studio market: a London 16-track room cost about £30/hour, while Spaceward (Cambridge) sold a 16-hour day (10am-2am) for about £100; Studio Sound (Oct 1976) quotes a new 16-track room at £27/hour - so a 4-hour demo ran about £100 plus tape
Includes: Studio time (engineering inclusion varies by quote)
Proposed gameplay use: Model cheap provincial studios vs expensive London rooms; full-day packages stretch budgets; prices demo sessions too
Notes / caveats: Trade quote: worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Audio/Archive-Studio-Sound/70s/Studio-Sound-1976-10.pdf

Finding: Iron Maiden could not afford the £50 2-inch master tape after their session; the studio later taped over it
Includes: Blank tape only
Proposed gameplay use: Tape is a separate cash cost after the session; losing the master is a natural fail state

Finding: The Jam signed to Polydor in Feb 1977 for £6,000 and a 6% royalty - the cleanest beginner-tier UK major-label anchor found; an option exercise across four albums/four years raised the rate to 13%
Includes: Signing advance; starting royalty; option escalation over 4 albums in 4 years
Proposed gameplay use: New-act major tier: £5-10k advances, 5-8% starting royalty; option-exercise event jumps the rate

Finding: Period royalty norms: UK 8-15%, US 5-12%; 'typical' artist royalty sat between 5-15% - new acts at the bottom of the range
Unit / coverage: Percentage of sales (base not stated in source)
Includes: n/a
Proposed gameplay use: Keep the major royalty band 5-15%; the game's 25%+ small-label tier is not evidenced for UK majors

Finding: Royalty base convention: artist share computed on ~90% of the retail selling price (period example, musician interview)
Includes: Illustrates the 90%-of-retail base convention
Proposed gameplay use: Royalty calculator default: rate x 0.9 x retail price x units
Notes / caveats: Base for UK majors remains inferred - unresolved list

Finding: Publishing norms: writers commonly assigned copyright for its full term on a 50:50 revenue split with the publisher, with no automatic reversion
Includes: Full-term copyright assignment; no reversion right
Proposed gameplay use: Publishing default: full-term assignment, 50:50 split, no reversion - escape only via rare events (F20)

Finding: Schroeder Music Publishing v Macaulay (House of Lords 1974): a standard-form publishing contract with an unknown songwriter (5-year term, £50 total advance, life-of-copyright assignment, auto-extension above £5,000 royalties) was held void as an unreasonable restraint of trade
Includes: Illustrates exploitative standard-form publishing terms of the era
Proposed gameplay use: Dispute event card: onerous contracts can be challenged in court; £50 is a litigated floor, not an average advance

Finding: Recoupment: advances are repaid from the artist's royalty share (not label gross); recording costs, video, tour support and some promotion are recoupable; the advance often doubles as the recording budget
Includes: Advance, recording costs, video, tour support, promotion
Proposed gameplay use: Recoupment basket UI: chart advance vs recording, video, tour-support and promo costs drawn from the artist share

Finding: Punk signing spree: Sex Pistols ~£40,000 (EMI, Oct 1976, dropped after ~3 months), then £75,000+ (A&M, Mar 1977, dropped in six days, kept the money); The Clash £100,000 (CBS, Jan 1977) - a ~16x spread over The Jam in the same year
Includes: Reported signing advances; terms disputed
Proposed gameplay use: Hype can multiply offers far beyond sales history; labels drop hype acts fast and severance stays with the artist
Notes / caveats: Famous acts - not beginner-representative; reported figures. Companion: ultimate-guitar.com/news/trends/the-sex-pistols-got-paid-by-four-different-labels-for-one-album

Finding: Management commission benchmarks: Beatles/Epstein contracts at 10-15% of income (1962), rising to 25% of gross income at the top end after renegotiation; managers of the day believed ~10% was the norm; adjacent 1975: AC/DC's manager on 20% of gross (Australia)
Includes: Commission on income, not royalties specifically
Proposed gameplay use: Manager commission: ~10% era norm with 20-25%-of-gross as aggressive upper end; do not backdate modern 15-25% as fact
Notes / caveats: No direct UK-1970s figure found - see unresolved list

Finding: Musicians' Union needle-time rules rationed records on BBC radio, so live sessions (John Peel) became a main on-air route for unknown bands: ~4,000 sessions for 2,000+ artists (1967-2004); demo tapes were a documented route in
Includes: Band records 3-4 tracks at BBC studio; broadcast on Peel's show
Proposed gameplay use: Peel session as low-cost national exposure gate for unsigned acts; demo submission a real, low-probability route

Finding: Sniffin' Glue grew from ~50 copies (issue 1, 1976) to 15,000 monthly circulation; the final issue ran 20,000 copies with a flexi-disc single funded by £90 left in the bank
Unit / coverage: Copies per issue; one-off print run
Includes: Photocopied/stapled zine; final issue incl. flexi-disc giveaway
Proposed gameplay use: Fanzine action: near-zero cost, fast-rising reach if it catches; can upgrade into a record-promotion vehicle
Notes / caveats: Issue-1 run (50) vs sales (~300, Christie's) unresolved

Finding: Music-press reach was mass media: NME ~136,000/week (1971) rising to ~230,000 (1980); Melody Maker peaked at 207,000 (1973); Sounds 128,000 (1972); Record Mirror 46,000 (1971) -> 136,000 (1980)
Includes: Audited ABC figures compiled from publisher reports
Proposed gameplay use: Press coverage carries six-figure reach - the largest single early-game promotion channel
Notes / caveats: Single compiled secondary source

Finding: TV was chart-gated: Top of the Pops slots tracked songs climbing the Top 40, so TV acts as a late-stage amplifier; exceptions like Granada's So It Goes gave unknowns (Sex Pistols) early national exposure (1976)
Includes: TV performance slot tied to chart position
Proposed gameplay use: Gate TOTP-class slots on chart position; add regional late-night TV as an early exposure route
Notes / caveats: Companion: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_It_Goes_(TV_series)

Finding: A new 16-track studio was quoted at £27/hour (Oct 1976), so a multi-hour demo was a serious outlay for a young band
Includes: 16-track studio hire (engineering inclusion unknown)
Proposed gameplay use: Price a demo session at ~£25-30/hour - a 4-hour demo roughly £100 plus tape

Finding: Label break-even: ~20,000 records for a mainstream rock album vs ~2,000 for a cheaply recorded pub-rock release - a 10x difference in viability
Includes: Cheap recording plus pressing for a small indie release
Source type: Encyclopedic summary (citing Dave Laing, One Chord Wonders)
Proposed gameplay use: Make low-cost recording an economically rational first-rung strategy: cheaper records need far fewer sales to break even

Finding: Stiff Records (1976, formed from a £400 loan) released the first UK punk single; Rough Trade launched a distribution arm and the regional 'Cartel' network formed around 1978, giving indie releases national shop reach
Includes: Label launch; distribution network
Proposed gameplay use: Indie infrastructure arrives 1976-78: DIY releases gain national distribution as a late-decade unlock
Notes / caveats: Cartel chronology contested; companion: crackmagazine.net/article/long-reads/rough-trade-feature

Finding: The first official independent chart was published 19 January 1980 - inside the 1970s there is no separate indie chart, so independent releases had to crack the main chart
Includes: Singles and albums charts
Proposed gameplay use: Era gate: indie-chart visibility begins in 1980, not in the 1970s

Finding: UK singles units hit successive records: 88.8m (1978) and 89.1m (1979, never beaten pre-digital) - singles did not collapse by units; the album side boomed in value (£163m vinyl album trade value peak, 1978)
Includes: UK trade deliveries; vinyl album trade value
Proposed gameplay use: Any late-decade 'singles decline' mechanic must be value/margin-driven, not unit-collapse
Notes / caveats: Album value companion: musicbusinessresearch.wordpress.com/2017/07/30/the-uk-recorded-music-market-in-a-long-term-perspective-1975-2016

Finding: Ian Curtis kept a civil-service day job at a Manpower Services Commission job centre while Joy Division gigged and recorded
Includes: Day job held alongside band activity
Proposed gameplay use: Member job state: weekday unavailability, small steady income, quit-job decision when the band breaks

Finding: Peter Gabriel left Genesis citing family time and the band's 'pseudo-democratic committee' unable to hold one clear direction
Includes: Family strain plus artistic-direction conflict
Proposed gameplay use: Family-strain and artistic-control events as distinct churn drivers
Notes / caveats: Famous act - not beginner-representative

Finding: Rolling Stones: Mick Taylor quit; he and Jagger denied credit/money motives while reports and his wife pointed to missing co-writing credit and lost royalties
Includes: Credit/royalty dispute reported but contested
Proposed gameplay use: Credit-split disputes drive churn; stated morale reasons may mask hidden money issues
Notes / caveats: Famous act - not beginner-representative; motive contested

Finding: Brewer's Droop (pub-rock band) played about 300 gigs in 1970 and close to 1,000 across the following four years
Includes: Gigs only
Proposed gameplay use: Benchmark annual gig count for a grinding working band; drives fatigue accumulation mechanics
Notes / caveats: Single source

Finding: Contemporary Music Week price anchors: singles 50p (Dec 1970, CBS) -> 63p avg (Oct 1975, price index of 18 majors, RRP incl. VAT) -> 70p 'normal' (Apr 1977); LPs £2.42 (Jul 1973) -> £2.45 (Nov 1974) -> £2.89 avg (Oct 1975) -> £3.49 (Feb 1977) -> £3.99 (Dec 1978) -> £4.99 (Jan 1980)
Includes: Retail list price, incl. VAT where stated; full-price product
Source type: Trade press scans (Music Week, multiple issues)
Proposed gameplay use: Retail price baseline for the game's price ladder; collector recollections of 45p/£2.50 (1974) fit discounted/budget tiers, not list
Notes / caveats: Gaps: 1971-72, 1976, 1978-79 singles. Full issue-level citations in evidence/resolution-prices-and-certification.md

Finding: BPI album awards were value-based from Apr 1973 (£1m platinum / £250k gold / £75k silver in 1974-75 keys; silver £100k from 1 Jan 1976; gold £300k / silver £150k for releases on/after 1 Jan 1977); unit thresholds (300,000 / 100,000 / 60,000) appear in trade keys 'as of Jan 1979'. Singles were unit-based throughout: 250,000 silver / 500,000 gold / 1,000,000 platinum
Includes: Shipment thresholds (basis of £ values contested: retail vs manufacturer revenue)
Source type: Trade press keys (Music Week scans) + chart historian archive
Proposed gameplay use: Certification events gated year-by-year: value-based awards 1973-78, unit-based from 1979; singles thresholds constant
Notes / caveats: BPI 'abolished Jan 1978' claim contradicted by trade keys - real switch late 1978/early 1979

Finding: The singles chart was a BMRB Top 50 from Feb 1969 (about 250 shops returning sales logs by post; sampling cost ~£52,000) and expanded to a Top 75 in May 1978
Unit / coverage: Chart sample of ~250 shops; chart size 50 -> 75
Includes: Chart compilation machinery
Proposed gameplay use: Chart entry is a sample estimate: small runs can chart or vanish on noise; entry gets easier from May 1978
Notes / caveats: Top 75 expansion per ultimatepopculture.fandom.com/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart

Finding: VAT on records: 10% from 1 Apr 1973, cut to 8% from 29 Jul 1974, 8% through 1979, 15% standard rate from 1979; before 1973 purchase tax sat on the wholesale price
Includes: Standard VAT rate; records treated as standard-rated
Proposed gameplay use: Higher VAT rate existed (25% then 12.5%) but records are standard-rated
Notes / caveats: Companion: taxadvisermagazine.com/article/vat-album (pre-1973 purchase tax on wholesale)
